newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lauds Fujimori on hostage crisis handling.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lauds Fujimori on hostage crisis handling.

text.p: Peru's President Alberto Fujimori discussed his handling of the Lima hostage crisis with President Bill Clinton on Monday and won Clinton's praise for "skillfully walking a very fine line" between firmness and humanitarian concern.

"The president told President Fujimori that he was skilfully walking a very fine line ... between resolving this crisis peacefully without giving in to terror," White House spokesman David Johnson said after a White House meeting of about 20 minutes. "He (Clinton) told him (Fujimori) that it is a hard line to walk but it's the right one."

Fujimori stopped off in Washington after an emergency weekend summit with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Toronto on Saturday. The 72 hostages have been held in the Japanese Embassy residence since Dec. 17 by Marxist rebels.
Johnson said the Clinton-Fujimori talk was also attended by Vice President Al Gore, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and National Security Adviser Samuel Berger.

Before the meeting, Fujimori dismissed suggestions of any "peace accord" with the hostage-takers. "Peru has paid too high a cost to impose law and order ... to throw it all overboard and give in to the extortion of a gaggle of human rights violators," he told the Organisation of American States, speaking in Spanish.

"Some people are starting to talk about a peace accord. We Peruvians do not understand what they are talking about, since that idea presumes a reality that is not Peru's. ... We do not understand what sort of peace accord they pretend (to impose) on a country that is living in peace. We are not going to accept such a peace agreement," he said.

Referring to the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels who are holding the hostages and demanding the release of jailed comrades, Fujimori said: "There are no guerrillas or popular armies in Peru, there is only a people tired of living in poverty and violence, a people who want to work and get ahead in life."

At their hastily arranged summit on Saturday, Fujimori and Hashimoto agreed to push for direct talks with the rebels but ruled out granting the guerrillas' demand for the liberation of about 400 jailed MRTA members. The rebels have also demanded improved prison conditions, an overhaul of Peru's secret court system for people accused of terrorism and an end to Fujimori's free-market economic reforms.

The leader of the MRTA, who is one of about 15 heavily armed guerrillas occupying the mansion in an upscale Lima neighbourhood, reiterated on Sunday that any government move to force them out would end in tragedy.

"We know (an assault by the Peruvian army) would be tragic for the gentlemen held captive here. We are sorry for them and for their families," Nestor Cerpa Cartolino said in an interview with two Spanish newspapers.

The rebels originally took more than 500 hostages during a cocktail party at the diplomatic mansion. Remaining captives in the mined and booby-trapped residence include two Peruvian government ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and Fujimori's brother.
